item.title: Mortgage Rates Remain High as Affordability Challenges Persist
item.description:
Mortgage rates slid for the fourth consecutive week but remain above 7 percent, adding pressure to a bleak housing market struggling with rising prices and declining sales.

The rate on the most popular home loan in the United States, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage, fell slightly to 7.11 percent, from 7.18 percent the week before, the mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac said on Thursday. The same rate averaged 6.24 percent a year ago.

There was hope that mortgage rates might ease below 7 percent, a psychological threshold that could draw more buyers to the market. But industry experts say that marker is not likely to be breached any time soon.

High housing costs have made buying a home unaffordable for many Americans, said Brad Case, the chief residential economist at Homes.com, a real estate search portal owned by CoStar, a data analytics company.

“I don’t think affordability challenges are going away any time soon,” he added, “because I don’t think we’re likely to see substantially lower mortgage rates.”

Squeezed by high mortgage rates and rising inflation, buyers and sellers are sitting out of the market until conditions improve, which has depressed home sales. Sales of existing homes fell 8.8 percent in October from the year before, and 5.5 percent lower than September’s pace, according to a report released Thursday by the National Association of Realtors, a trade group.

Existing-home sales have fallen to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, their slowest since August 2010, the NAR report said. A healthy annual sales pace is typically about five million existing homes.

“It’s a tough market for buyers and sellers,” Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist, said Thursday on a call with reporters, adding that the sales outlook for 2026 is looking increasingly gloomy. “It could be one of the lowest annual figures, once we tally up the final three months of this year,” he said.

Affordability challenges are likely to keep sales low for the next few months, said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. a listings website.

“I don’t think this is a new normal for home sales,” she said in a statement. “Instead, it reflects a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season.”

The housing market began to lock up in 2022, when mortgage rates started to climb after falling below 3 percent. Homeowners who snagged the ultralow rates have been unwilling to sell, which has put the market in a prolonged gridlock.

“You are going to have a frozen housing market for a long time,” said Jeff Ostrowski, housing market analyst at Bankrate, a consumer financial services company. “It’s been, I think, even more dramatic than anyone expected, just because mortgage rates went up so much.”

Mortgage rates fell below 6 percent the last week of February, giving hope that the housing market might rebound, but they began rising again after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. The war, which has lasted more than eight months, has driven up costs for fuel and food.

Consumer prices rose sharply in October, climbing 0.4 percent after a 0.6 percent increase in September. But wage growth has not kept pace, and home buyers are feeling the pinch because they have less to put toward a home.

“For affordability to get better, what really needs to happen is income growth,” Mr. Case of Homes.com said.

The jump in inflation has increased the odds that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its next meeting in December, which could put upward pressure on mortgage rates. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which underpins consumer loans like mortgages, climbed above 5 percent after the inflation report was released on Tuesday.

item.title: Microsoft Programs Disrupted by Outage
item.description:
Microsoft reported an outage involving its sprawling set of software tools early Thursday afternoon. The outage has continued for at least three hours, users reported.

Between 12:15 and 1 p.m. Eastern, the outage tracker Downdetector showed that more than 130,000 users were experiencing problems with Microsoft Outlook, which is used for email, calendars and other online tasks. Similar spikes in outages were reported with Microsoft 365, the workplace messaging app Microsoft Teams, the A.I. assistant Microsoft Copilot and the Microsoft Store, Downdetector’s data showed.

By 4 p.m. the number of users reporting issues with Microsoft’s applications had been cut nearly in half.

Microsoft said initially that part of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load.”

Later the company said in a social media post that “we determined the elevated load isn’t driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, straining the remaining infrastructure.”

“We’re working to safely return them to service,” Microsoft added in the post.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Democrats Eye Strict New Limits on White House Budget Powers
item.description:
Nearly two years ago, Democrats could do little more than watch as President Trump seized control of the U.S. budget, slashing billions of dollars and firing droves of civil workers in a downsizing that Congress never authorized.

Now, as the party prepares to take charge in the House and Senate, its incoming leaders say they are plotting ways to keep Mr. Trump in check.

In the wake of their overwhelming electoral victory, Democrats have promised to cement their power under the Constitution to control the nation’s purse. They hope to boost funding for federal climate, education, health, housing and safety net initiatives next year, then take steps that would prevent Mr. Trump from slowing down or interfering with the money again.

Many of these programs have experienced steep cuts and disruptions during Mr. Trump’s second term, as the White House embraces an expansive view of its power to override Congress. Even though lawmakers have approved the money, Mr. Trump has often refused to spend it or has used the funds for other purposes, drawing rebukes in court — and, on rare occasion, from some Republicans.

Democrats also plan to investigate the architect of that strategy: Russell T. Vought, the White House budget chief who has been working on a “fiscal consolidation” plan that could involve additional cuts, according to other officials.

Over the past two years, Mr. Vought has frequently tried to rebuff congressional oversight of his budget activities. And the White House on Thursday appeared to be considering one of Mr. Vought’s deputies for a post whose responsibilities include monitoring the budget office’s handling of federal spending.

“We’re going to ask Russ Vought a lot of questions,” said Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, adding that Congress would reassert its authorities and aim to “Trump-proof” its spending bills.

The plans reflect a broader reckoning on Capitol Hill, where the outgoing Republican majority had largely acquiesced to the Trump administration’s whims. But for Democrats, the task still may not be easy: Even with healthy margins in the House and Senate, they still would require some G.O.P. support to override a veto from Mr. Trump.

“I know there are people who are interested in these areas and want to reclaim the power of the purse,” said Representative Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the senior Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee.

Ms. DeLauro added that she was hopeful Democrats would be able to work with Republicans. But she also made clear that Democrats would seek to curtail Mr. Trump in other ways, if necessary, even if it meant Congress taking legal action against the administration.

“We can go to the courts,” she said, adding that the party would “look for every conceivable tool to thwart their efforts.”

For Mr. Trump, the roughly $2 trillion approved annually by Congress has become a political cudgel. He and his aides have adopted the view that they have immense power to reprogram federal spending as they see fit, triggering countless lawsuits that have often found that the administration broke the law.

Over the past two years, the president has frequently moved around money to accomplish his personal goals, whether it is to fund the construction of his White House ballroom or to pay immigration agents during a federal shutdown. He has also struck entire categories of spending — in science, education and foreign aid — simply because funding programs and their recipients were not aligned with his political views.

At one point, the White House proposed subjecting nearly every federal grant to a political litmus test, an idea that proved so objectionable that Republicans later joined Democrats to block it. And the administration has repeatedly weaponized the budget to deny federal aid to Democrats, a threat that Mr. Trump repeated on Thursday.

At the center of that strategy is Mr. Vought, who reprised his role as the leader of the Office of Management and Budget with the goal of slashing spending seen as “woke,” merging socially conservative values and the perennial Republican interest in austerity.

The president’s budgets, prepared by Mr. Vought, have twice called on Congress to make drastic cuts across most domestic programs, especially in science and those that aid the poor. In both cases, lawmakers rejected the White House blueprints, only to see Mr. Vought try to carry out some of the cuts on his own.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Mr. Vought has argued for years that he is acting within the law.

Daniel Kowalski, a former O.M.B. official in the Trump administration who now directs a budget center for the right-leaning Heritage Foundation, said he expected that pattern to continue even as Democrats prepared to assume their new majorities.

“I think there’s going to be a little bit of a cat-and-mouse game,” said Mr. Kowalski. “The Democrats are going to try to limit, and the administration is going to try to work around.”

That was evident within days of the election. In a pair of interviews, the two Democrats overseeing the annual appropriations process said that they had a number of such limits in mind.

Ms. DeLauro and Ms. Murray each said they would leverage their power over funding to fight what they described as Mr. Trump’s corruption, while aiming to restrict his policies, particularly his ability to carry out the war with Iran.

The two Democrats said they were especially interested in protecting the National Institutes of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, whose grants face strict political scrutiny in the Trump administration.

Ms. DeLauro said the approach had allowed the president and his aides to “run rampant over science and research,” undermining U.S. programs to develop cutting-edge cures. She added that Democrats believed they had a “mandate from this election” to fight back.

Democrats also hope to make it harder for the administration to cut or transfer spending without congressional permission. That includes closing off a loophole that allowed Mr. Vought to hold up billions of dollars in health, education and foreign aid at the end of the last two fiscal years, effectively causing the funds to expire, even though lawmakers never agreed to such a cut.

The tactic is known as a pocket rescission, and Mr. Vought insists it is legal. The White House budget chief has also supported the idea that the president can refuse to spend appropriated money altogether, a move known as impoundment, which is illegal.

Democrats said they planned to toughen up those restrictions on impoundment, and Ms. Murray said the party would couple its new rules with unspecified “penalties for breaking our laws” on spending.

The new strictures on the president would build on the more limited reforms that Democrats worked with Republicans to enact over the past year. The technical changes generally sought to force the White House to spend the amounts that Congress had dictated on paper.

Republicans otherwise had resisted more serious constraints on the president’s budgetary powers, and the White House largely shrugged off the rules, prompting another round of court battles. But the moment illustrated the growing, bipartisan discord with Mr. Vought.

The outrage has hardly deterred the White House.

As soon as this week, the president is expected to nominate a new comptroller general who would lead the Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog that is responsible for overseeing the administration’s handling of federal spending. It carries a 15-year term, replacing Gene Dodaro, who retired when his term expired at the end of last year.

The administration has eyed Eric Ueland, a top O.M.B. official, to take the post, according to two people familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss plans that were not finalized. If the president proceeds, and the Senate confirms him, it would put in place an ally of Mr. Vought’s in a role that helps to oversee the budget director.

The Washington Sun previously reported on the possible nomination.

In an unorthodox move, Republicans this week raced to start the nomination process before they had formally received a nominee. The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee merely listed the position — without a name — for an initial hearing on Nov. 19.

A spokesman for Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the panel, did not respond to a request for comment. The move angered Democratic leaders, including Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, both of New York, who in a joint statement criticized Mr. Trump for trying to “install a fox in the henhouse.”

“I absolutely expect that O.M.B. will continue to abuse its authority to withhold funds for the programs the administration disfavors,” said Cerin Lindgrensavage, who serves as a counsel at Protect Democracy, a group that has repeatedly, and successfully, sued the administration over its budget tactics.

Ms. Lindgrensavage said she would “expect that problem to get worse and not better until Congress creates real consequences for O.M.B.”

item.title: Looking Past Nvidia Turmoil, Stocks Log Best Week in Months
item.description:
The stock market on Friday was set for its best week in months, as investors brushed off concerns about the resignation of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia, the behemoth chip maker.

The S&P 500 is on course to rise more than 3 percent for the week, which would be its best five-day stretch since early August. The Nasdaq Composite has also risen more than 3 percent so far this week.

The moves are an end to weeks of losses in which concerns about a slowdown in the growth of the artificial intelligence industry weighed on the market and prompted sharp sell-offs in many of the tech companies that have led the market higher in recent years.

“The market is in an incredibly good position to move higher,” said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for the investment management arm at Nationwide, an insurance company. “Once you get through the news-driven sentiment, you can get back to focusing on fundamentals. That is hopefully what we are seeing.”

The market was on edge after revelations that Mr. Huang, a standard-bearer for the A.I. revolution, had engaged in an extramarital affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

After reports that Mr. Huang had a second affair, this time with a subordinate employee, Nvidia’s board announced the chief executive’s departure on Thursday morning, a dramatic fall from grace for the tech mogul. Nvidia’s shares dropped on Thursday, and its stock is now about 30 percent below its all-time high, set just over a month ago. The company, which is the second-largest member of the S&P 500 index, behind Apple, is trading about 12 percent lower for the year.

Importantly, analysts said, Nvidia’s big drop has not spread to the rest of the market. Rival chip makers’ stocks have risen, as have A.I. stocks more broadly. As of Friday morning, major indexes remain on course to record their first weekly gain in more than a month, with futures indicating a relatively subdued open to trading in New York. Nvidia’s stock reversed some of its losses in premarket trading, rising about 2 percent.

“We doubt the fundamentals supporting the A.I. industrial revolution are altered by Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia,” analysts at Raymond James, a financial services company, said, adding that “‘hate selling’ is understandable, but objectively, fundamentals appear to have changed very little.”

Analysts who cover Nvidia have been adjusting their expectations this week, based on forecasts compiled by Bloomberg. While many analysts have cut their share price targets sharply, they still expect the stock to trade markedly higher than where it currently trades, at around $166.

Harlan Sur at JPMorgan lowered his price target for the company to $215 from $320 over the summer. Atif Malik at Citi lowered his to $225 from $315 earlier this month. Karl Ackerman at BNP Paribas has kept his target at $345.

Stock investors have also brushed off a sharp rise in interest rates this week, driven higher by data showing U.S. consumer prices rising more quickly than expected.

The 10-year Treasury yield, which underpins interest rates for mortgages, business loans and other types of debt throughout the economy, has risen more than 0.2 percentage points so far this week, on course for one of its highest moves of the year.

Investors now expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at least 0.75 percentage points over the next 12 months, starting with a quarter-point raise in December. A week ago, investors were forecasting just one quarter-point increase over the same period.

The two-year Treasury yield, which is sensitive to changes in expectations for Fed rate moves, has risen more than 0.3 percentage points higher this week, its largest one-week rise in more than four years.

Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, said on Thursday that the central bank needed “to move to a restrictive stance of policy to help bring inflation back down,” meaning a need to raise interest rates further.

“If we don’t,” she added, “I worry ​that an inflationary mind-set could start taking hold.”

item.title: Jensen Huang’s Fall Costs Asia an A.I. Ambassador to the U.S.
item.description:
In Indonesia, Jensen Huang was called the leader of the artificial intelligence revolution. In Japan, he was “the next Steve Jobs,” according to the technology investor Masayoshi Son. In Taiwan, where he was born, he is just called Dad.

Mr. Huang, who resigned this week from the powerhouse Silicon Valley chip company Nvidia, was celebrated across Asia — from South Korea to Japan, Indonesia to Kazakhstan. He traveled frequently to the region, cultivating close ties with business leaders and wooing government officials.

Outside of China, he pitched Nvidia chips as a path to “sovereign A.I.,” the idea that countries had to build their own A.I. supercomputers and data centers, a vision that many government leaders bought into.

Even in China, where the business relationships he forged for Nvidia were made more complicated by the rivalry between Beijing and Washington, Mr. Huang was often seen as a bridge. That role was cast in a new light by the explosive revelations about his relationship with a woman the U.S. government believes was spying for China.

Nvidia is valued at about $4 trillion, one of the largest corporate valuations in the world. Now Mr. Huang’s sudden departure from the company hangs over the region’s technology industry, raising questions about what it portends for the region’s A.I. boom, U.S. policy on China and the continued expansion of data centers in Southeast Asia, where Nvidia chips power A.I. development throughout the region.

For China, Mr. Huang’s exit could accelerate a drive toward self-sufficiency as Beijing and Chinese companies fear Washington will tighten export controls on American-designed chips.

Many Chinese companies use data centers in Malaysia and other countries to access chips they would not otherwise be able to bring into China. In recent days, Chinese companies in Malaysia have begun racing to lease space inside data centers with advanced American-designed A.I. chips before any new restrictions can be put in place, said a data center executive in Malaysia, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing efforts.

China had already been positioning itself to be self-sufficient in chips, but many of its companies doing frontier A.I. development relied on Nvidia chips. Mr. Huang’s resignation has pushed up the timeline, according to analysts.

“The Chinese A.I. industry must prepare for the worst-case scenario: pairing domestic chips with domestic models and building a complete, self-contained ecosystem,” said Zhong Yang, an investor focused on A.I. who is based in Guangdong Province, in an email.

Companies could soon face an “existential necessity” to replace foreign chips with ones made in China, he said.

In China, Mr. Huang was seen as a moderating force on contentious questions about access to advanced technology. He has long argued that strict U.S. export controls would open the doors for more Chinese competition. He has said exporting the “American tech stack” is vital to winning the A.I. race and that the blocking of chip exports forces China away from American technology.

“His departure means that China has lost an influential advocate within the U.S. tech sector for business cooperation,” said Poe Zhao, an independent China technology analyst.

Mr. Zhao said he believes that Mr. Huang’s resignation could hurt China’s A.I. industry in the short term, but may benefit domestic chip manufacturers such as Huawei. But he pointed out that Chinese-made chips still lag in performance.

“In the long run, whether China can benefit depends on whether domestically produced chips can truly narrow the technological gap,” he added.

Joe Mazur, a senior analyst at Trivium China, a consultancy, said Mr. Huang’s departure could “embolden the voices in Washington that are less in favor of cooperation, more in favor of a hard-line approach.”

Over time, Mr. Huang’s departure is a “dream scenario for China,” said Dan Ives, a prominent technology analyst on Wall Street.

“The biggest gating factor between the U.S. and China was Jensen and Nvidia,” Mr. Ives said.

One of the distinguishing features of Mr. Huang’s role in the Asia tech world was his ability to cultivate personal relationships with Nvidia’s suppliers that kept a steady stream of critical components flowing to the company.

Last year, with the industry starting to face a shortage of the high-speed memory chips that work alongside Nvidia’s A.I. semiconductors, Mr. Huang embarked on a charm offensive aimed at the leaders of South Korea’s two memory chip giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

Now South Korea is fretting about the future of those joint business projects, which are valued at about $510 billion. It is also concerned about Washington’s export controls on China, which accounts for 40 percent of the semiconductors that South Korea exports.

“It is no exaggeration to say that the semiconductor supercycle we are currently riding is thanks to the A.I. ecosystem cultivated by Nvidia,” the Korea Economic Daily wrote in an editorial. “While one might argue that these are merely risks to be born by the C.E.O. personally, the issue lies in the fact that ‘Jensen Huang is, in effect, Nvidia itself.’”

In Southeast Asia, Mr. Huang’s departure “would put a damper on demand for A.I. compute in existing and future data centers,” according to Ong Kian Ming, Malaysia’s former deputy minister for investment, trade and industry.

“Malaysia would take the brunt of the likely drop in demand, but this may also have spillover effects on Thailand and Indonesia,” Mr. Ong said.

On Friday, Malaysia said it was working to determine whether any A.I. chips imported by ​a unit of Megaspeed were re-exported. Megaspeed is the Singapore-based firm that is run by Alice Huang, the woman who had a relationship with Mr. Huang and who U.S. intelligence has determined was spying for China. China has denied the espionage claims. Megaspeed said in a statement that it has cooperated with U.S. government inspections and will continue to do so. Ms. Huang hasn’t been able to be reached.

Mr. Huang was a rare chief executive who huddled with business titans over fried chicken and beer and mingled with the public while eating street food. He made it a point to meet many Asian officials on his trips, including China’s leader, Xi Jinping.

“What Southeast Asia will struggle to find is another Nvidia boss willing to fly in, sit down with its prime ministers and argue its case in Washington,” wrote Jude Chan, a journalist from The Business Times, a Singapore newspaper, which called Mr. Huang “Nvidia’s best salesman.”

Mr. Huang was seen as a megastar in Taiwan. His visits to Taipei are typically live streamed for hours at a time. The domestic media frenzy that surrounds his visits have been called “Jensanity.”

He has met regularly with executives from TSMC, the Taiwanese giant that manufactures chips. He has hosted banquets for his Taiwanese suppliers, and is known particularly for his close relationship with TSMC’s founder, Morris Chang.

In Japan, which Mr. Huang visited in July, Mr. Huang said the country could use its prowess in manufacturing and industrial robots to become a leader in sovereign development of physical A.I. All it needed was to install tens of thousands of Nvidia chips.

Japan’s economy minister, Ryosei Akazawa, and dozens of Japanese corporate leaders attended a launch event in Tokyo for a tech consortium to build these physical A.I. models.

Mr. Akazawa wore a black leather jacket. He told the audience his clothing choice was meant to express his “great respect” for Mr. Huang, who made leather jackets his signature look.

Forty-four major Japanese companies ended up joining the consortium, including Sony Group, SoftBank, NEC and Honda. Share prices of companies whose executives reportedly shared meals with Mr. Huang on his Tokyo trip surged.

At the time, analysts and researchers also questioned whether the state-backed initiative would actually further sovereign Japanese A.I. or just create a risky dependency on a single foreign company: Nvidia.

Li You and Choe Sang-Hun contributed reporting from Seoul, Zunaira Saieed from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and Alexandra Stevenson from Hong Kong.

item.title: Deed Theft Is Going Up as Rising Values Make Homes a Lucrative Target
item.description:
A dying woman with dementia. A doctor from Long Island. A couple renovating a home in Florida.

The three fell victim to a type of real estate fraud known as deed, or title, theft, in which someone forges documents or fakes an identity to take ownership of a home or vacant land. Criminals may impersonate the true owners and sell the property to unsuspecting buyers, or use it as collateral to obtain loans.

The rise in home property values, and, therefore, home equity, have made deed theft potentially lucrative, experts say. Homes owned by older people, homes that show signs of financial distress, and vacant homes or land may be especially vulnerable.

It’s not clear how common deed theft is nationally but awareness of the fraud is mounting, especially in the Northeast. Earlier this month, a Queens man became the first person convicted under a New York deed theft law passed in 2024. And New York City has created a special office of deed theft prevention to detect and investigate such fraud.

Reports of real estate crime in general rose by 32 percent in 2025, to more than 12,000 complaints, and associated financial losses rose to more than $275 million, according to the F.B.I.’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. The F.B.I. estimates it received 66 complaints about deed or title theft in 2025, representing $5.9 million in losses, compared with 75 complaints representing losses of almost $7 million from January through October of this year.

The National Association of Realtors surveyed real-estate executives nationally in 2025 and found that nearly two-thirds reported being aware of this type of fraud in their area within the past year, with awareness highest — 95 percent — in the Northeast.

But the fraud isn’t confined to one region. “It happens everywhere,” said Craig Haskins, president of the American Land Title Association, a trade group for title insurers and agents and real-estate closing professionals. The group’s survey this year of 245 title professionals in 40 states found that nearly three out of five had experienced at least one incident of attempted “seller impersonation” fraud, up from about a quarter two years earlier.

Here’s what to know about deed theft and related fraud.

In a common scenario, thieves file a deed on a home or property to transfer ownership to themselves, often by forging the true owner’s signature or duping the owner into signing it.

In the recent case in Queens, a man pleaded guilty to stealing the home of an older woman with dementia in 2024 by forging her signature on a deed giving ownership of the home where she had lived for 40 years, and where she was receiving home care, to himself and an accomplice. The fake signature was also notarized with a forged signature. They next forged her signature on another deed transferring the home to his business, which he used to take out a $552,500 mortgage. He then paid off the owner’s mortgage and other liens, allowing him to steal the balance of more than $300,000 for his “personal benefit,” according to prosecutors.

The theft was discovered by the owner’s son and daughter-in-law when they opened suspicious mail at her home. As a result of the plea agreement, the home will be returned to the family of the woman, who died in 2025, according to the New York State attorney general’s office. (The accomplice’s trial is scheduled for early next year.)

That can vary. In New York City, complaints have been concentrated in Brooklyn and Queens, where criminals often target seniors and immigrants, and homes in historically Black neighborhoods. Deirdre Lok, director and managing attorney at the Weinberg Center for Elder Justice in Riverdale, N.Y., said someone who bought a brownstone in the 1970s or ’80s may not realize they own an asset now worth millions. (Clips from The New York Times show such homes could be purchased for $25,000 or $35,000, and sometimes even less.)

The situation can be complicated by “tangled title” properties, in which a home is passed down to heirs informally, with multiple people having ownership, or lacking clear documentation of ownership. That can make it difficult for owners to borrow against the home, and may make them more vulnerable to lowball offers from scammers, according to a study by New York University’s Furman Center.

In other areas, vacant land or unoccupied homes can be attractive to criminals because owners aren’t nearby to notice any changes or suspicious activity.

“Older people are more likely to own their own home and to have paid it off, and they are more likely to have a second home,” which may not be occupied year round, said Françoise Cleveland, government relations adviser with AARP.

Dreama Bilby, 77, and her husband, Larry, 79, said in an interview that they had moved out of their house in Tampa, Fla., years ago after a large tree fell on it. They relocated to an apartment, intending to eventually rebuild. But the Bilbys became worried when security cameras installed near the house spotted a man and woman they didn’t recognize stopping by the property. Their concern turned to alarm when the woman identified herself to a neighbor as the home’s new occupant. It turned out thieves had filed a fraudulent deed in February 2024, transferring ownership from the Bilbys. The thieves eventually pleaded guilty to criminal charges, according to the state attorney’s office in Hillsborough County, which includes Tampa.

“That was such a traumatic experience,” Ms. Bilby said in an interview. “It really did a number on me.”

In another vacant property case, a Long Island doctor was surprised when a neighbor reported in 2023 that a large home was being built on a wooded lot the doctor owned in Fairfield, Conn. It turned out that someone had used a forged power of attorney and fake documents in 2022 to fraudulently sell the land for $350,000 to an unsuspecting developer. A lawsuit filed in the case was settled in 2024.

Many counties or local governments now offer free services that automatically notify property owners if any documents are filed related to their property. (The Bilbys said they were able to halt the transfer of the deed on their home before it became final, because they had signed up for alerts.)

If your county doesn’t offer electronic deed alerts, you can periodically check your property records. Most areas now offer online search tools.

If you are buying a home, consider purchasing owners’ title insurance, Mr. Haskins said. Lender title insurance protects the mortgage lender on a home purchase against any undiscovered liens on the property or gaps in the chain of ownership. Banks typically require it if you are financing the purchase of a home. But buyers can also ask about paying for optional coverage, either as an add-on or with a separate policy that protects them, including against fraud.

Be certain to specify what type of coverage you are seeking. Some policies provide protection only for fraud that occurred before the closing. Others can protect for fraud that occurs after you become the owner. Availability may vary by state.

Typically, owner premiums are charged as a one-time payment, based on a percentage of the home’s purchase price. Costs vary by state and by the home’s selling price. For example, Mr. Haskins said, an owner’s policy in Wisconsin on a home priced at $338,200, the state median, would be about $1,439, or 0.43 percent of the purchase price. In Florida, the cost for a home at the state median price of about $416,800 would be about $1,610, or about 0.39 percent.

Be cautious about commercial services that promise to “lock” the title to your property for a fee. The Federal Trade Commission has warned that “title lock” services are not insurance and essentially charge for alerts that government services offer free.

Other tips: Pay close attention to your mail and email. If you stop receiving regular tax and utility bills or get bills that seem odd — say, a high water bill from a vacant property — check and make sure nothing is amiss.

If you own property you can’t visit regularly, consider having a friendly neighbor check on it for you.

item.title: Fewer Fed Meetings Raise Stakes of Warsh’s Communications
item.description:
When officials at the Federal Reserve meet next month to vote on interest rates, they will have only a partial snapshot of the economy in hand. Fresh inflation data comes out the day after policymakers finalize their rate decision, leaving them without insight into whether price pressures in November continued to accelerate or showed signs of easing.

This predicament underscores why officials at the central bank broadly appear on board with a plan hatched by Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, to reduce the number of meetings convened each year to vote on interest rates.

The changes will be ushered in gradually, beginning next fall. In a revised schedule released on Thursday, the Fed confirmed that its policymakers will meet eight times in 2027, but that the Oct. 25-26 gathering will be “dedicated to the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues.”

By 2028, there will be just six meetings accompanied by policy votes, with two others focused on strategy.

Meeting less frequently, and at more evenly spaced intervals, has the clear benefit of giving officials a more consistent flow of economic data to parse when they gather to debate their policy settings. But there are trade-offs that will put more onus on Mr. Warsh to communicate openly about how the Fed is approaching its rate decisions and its thinking about the outlook, something he has so far resisted even as the central bank has embarked on raising rates this year.

“The decision process is more important than the timing,” said Esther George, who served as president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City from 2011 to 2023. “And this committee is struggling a bit with how to communicate what exactly they mean.”

Since taking over as chairman in May, Mr. Warsh has embraced a different communications style than his predecessors. He has been much more circumspect about what he is willing to share, keeping his views about the economy close to his chest, as well as anything related to the policy outlook. That has resulted in occasional public remarks and abridged news conferences.

In fact, one of his first acts as chairman was to overhaul the Fed’s policy statement that accompanies rate decisions. It now is significantly shorter and less detailed.

The void has been filled by Mr. Warsh’s colleagues, who have continued to vocalize their thinking about how the economy is faring; the extent of the inflation problem that the Fed is facing; and often very explicitly, what the central bank should do with rates to address it.

The dynamic reared up this week in the wake of new inflation data that showed price pressures intensifying more than expected. Officials from across the Fed engaged in what amounted to a public debate about how aggressive the central bank now needs to be in squeezing the economy to get inflation under control.

For William English, a former director of the Fed’s monetary affairs division who is now a professor at Yale University, Mr. Warsh’s communications style is a consequential one that will grow more pronounced as the Fed meets more sparingly.

“He’s giving up a fair amount by communicating as little as he seems to want to communicate, and I worry that’s really not helpful for the public’s understanding of what the committee is trying to achieve,” said Mr. English.

“If you had a committee that was meeting really often, then you don’t necessarily have to communicate as much, because you’re going to be taking another step or not taking another step very soon,” he added. “The longer the gap, the more communication does matter.”

At the turn of next year, for example, there will be a roughly two-month gap between policy votes. According to the new schedule, the Fed’s final gathering, typically scheduled for December, will be on Nov. 16-17, 2027. Officials would next meet Jan. 25-26, 2028, if the tentative schedule holds. Notably, the Fed’s rate moves in the last three years have mostly been in the final quarter of the year.

Fewer gatherings raise the prospects that the Fed will have to move in bigger increments than its typical quarter-point pace to play catch-up if the economic backdrop changes rapidly between rate decisions. It could also mean that impromptu meetings, which in the past have been reserved for crises, might happen more regularly.

Each of these dramatic steps could potentially create a lot of havoc for financial markets if not properly explained. Clearer communication could also help the Fed avoid taking them in the first place, said Donald Kohn, who served as vice-chair of the Fed from 2006 and 2010 when Mr. Warsh was a governor.

If the Fed provided guidance that it was worried about the inflation backdrop, for example, markets would begin to price in additional policy tightening if the data came in worse than expected. “But, if you’re not telling the markets about what you’re worried about and how you’re viewing things, they’re not going to have the ability to get out ahead of you,” said Mr. Kohn.

The meeting schedule is just one facet of a broader overhaul that Mr. Warsh wants in how the Fed communicates. One of five task forces he formed is looking at the range of tools at the central bank’s disposal: from the release of quarterly economic projections by officials known as the “dot plot,” which Mr. Warsh has openly criticized, to the post-policy meeting news conferences and minutes that are released three weeks later.

Kurt Lewis, a former senior Fed adviser who is now head of central bank policy at the investment bank Piper Sandler, said he expects sweeping changes to the dot plot. He anticipates that it could be replaced by some form of an economic forecast, potentially provided by Fed staff instead of policymakers.

Changes to the dot plot would likely require the support of Mr. Warsh’s colleagues. But the chairman would have unilateral authority to decide how often he wants to hold news conferences, for example.

For Mr. Lewis, one thing is probably off limits no matter how much Mr. Warsh’s wants it to change: “No one is going to agree to talk less.”

item.title: Silicon Valley Start-Ups Face a Future Without Jensen Huang’s Money
item.description:
For years, Jensen Huang was a frequent presence at Silicon Valley start-up events, networking with founders, judging pitch competitions and showing up at “demo” days.

The Nvidia chief executive became a godlike figure in the start-up ecosystem, not just because the industry idolized him as one of the world’s most successful entrepreneurs. Mr. Huang, 63, also made it his mission to help start-ups gain a foothold against the industry’s biggest and most powerful tech companies, providing funding and computing power.

“As many good ideas as we have, you don’t have all the world’s good ideas,” he said on the Acquired podcast in 2023.

So Mr. Huang’s abrupt resignation from Nvidia on Thursday has investors and start-up founders nervous that they have lost a powerful ally.

“Nvidia is the central bank of A.I. and all of a sudden, the Fed chairman is out,” said Tomasz Tunguz, an investor at Theory Ventures, which funds young start-ups.

Nvidia held $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including large stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July, according to securities filings. It more than doubled its start-up investments in six months.

Perhaps more critically, Nvidia has provided start-ups and small companies with access to A.I. chips that would have been difficult for them to obtain otherwise, offering $165 billion in lease guarantees and other backstops for cloud computing to start-ups and other companies, according to securities filings. The company has a venture capital arm and a program called Inception that provides tens of thousands of start-ups with training and guidance on how to access chips and computing power.

Mr. Huang has also been the industry’s most vocal advocate for “open source” and “open weight” technology, which makes underlying A.I. technology freely available for anyone to use, which benefits start-ups. Nvidia shelled out nearly $20 billion to buy two open source-focused companies in the last year.

Mr. Huang’s departure adds more uncertainty to an already jittery market. Investors fear A.I. is in a bubble that could burst. And the tech industry also faces potential regulation and a slowdown in data center construction ushered in by the results of the midterm elections. Nvidia controls the vast majority of the world’s market for the computer chips that A.I. companies need to build and service their technology.

The change in leadership could make it more difficult for smaller companies to access the chips and cloud computing power they need to compete against well-funded tech giants like Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft. More practically, it throws a number of investment deals Nvidia has in the works into limbo.

Mike Volpi, an investor at Hanabi Capital, a venture capital firm that backs A.I. companies, said he expected to Nvidia to take a more conservative approach to backstopping so many smaller cloud companies.

“My expectation is that we will see some turbulence and some of Nvidia funds coming out of the market in the short term,” he said.

The A.I. industry relies so much on Nvidia that commentators have started to caution against the risks.

Speaking to a standing-room-only audience of software developers in San Francisco last month before Mr. Huang came under fire, Dylan Patel, who runs SemiAnalysis, an A.I. research firm, warned that struggling young data center companies were having no problem securing revenue guarantees from Nvidia. That allowed the companies to then take on debt they otherwise wouldn’t have gotten.

“This is sort of a quite a risky proposition,” Mr. Patel said. “We’ll see what ends up happening there.”

Mr. Huang’s pro-start-up stance has delivered cash windfalls to venture capital investors over the past year, especially with Nvidia’s purchases of start-ups. The company bought the technology and hired employees from chipmaker Groq for roughly $20 billion last December and the A.I. open-source platform Hugging Face for about $14 billion in September.

“Jensen Huang, we have yet to meet, but bravo!” Joseph T. Hasselmann, a start-up investor who backed Groq, wrote on LinkedIn after the deal was announced.

Samantha Lau, who manages a tech stock portfolio at AllianceBernstein, an investment firm, said Mr. Huang’s exit would probably eliminate a key source of financing for companies like the young data center firms that have been planning public offerings, and dampen overall market enthusiasm.

“The god of circular financing is going into hibernation,” she said, referring to the A.I. industry’s many interconnected deals.

Sujay Jaswa, a partner at Wndr, a venture capital firm that has hosted Mr. Huang as its events, compared his resignation to the death of Steve Jobs.

“It’s a gigantic loss for all of us,” he said.

item.title: Bessent Faults Commerce Dept. for Failing to Blacklist Megaspeed
item.description:
Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, blamed the Commerce Department on Friday for the government’s failure to sanction the Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed, saying that other departments had pushed for the measure but that Commerce “has the pen.”

The Treasury, Defense and State Departments and the U.S. trade representative were all in favor of putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist called the entity list for months, but the Commerce Department is in charge of that authority, Mr. Bessent said on CNBC on Friday.

“You will have to have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said, adding, “Treasury and my deputy has been pushing for this for months at the deputies level.”

“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies,” he said. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

Frustration is boiling over within the administration and on Capitol Hill about Megaspeed, the company led by a woman U.S. intelligence deemed to be an asset for the Chinese government.

The woman, Alice Huang, had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang. Mr. Huang resigned from his company on Thursday in the wake of revelations about that and another affair, sending the company’s stock price cratering.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with other officials in recent months over technology exports, which his department oversees. He has urged caution on sweeping export restrictions and recommended more surgical action, drawing accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that his department has become too cozy with Nvidia and Mr. Huang.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Mr. Bessent had confronted Mr. Lutnick last week over his handling of Megaspeed, demanding to know why the United States had not already banned sales of advanced A.I. chips to the firm. Mr. Lutnick said he would move quickly to put restrictions on Megaspeed in place, people briefed on the exchange said.

The move to blacklist Megaspeed had been discussed earlier at a meeting of the deputies of cabinet officials, where Jeffrey Kessler, an under secretary in the Commerce Department, deferred on taking action, saying that the decision was up to Mr. Lutnick, the people said.

A spokeswoman for the Commerce Department denied that the conversation between Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick took place. She said that the decision about whether to add companies to the entity list was an administration-wide one. The Treasury Department did not comment.

Mr. Bessent questioned on Friday what Mr. Huang and Nvidia had known about Megaspeed’s business, and suggested that Nvidia should be held accountable if it did not have adequate oversight.

Megaspeed bought Nvidia chips to set up data centers in Southeast Asia that serve Chinese clients, a legal loophole in U.S. export controls. Both the Trump administration and Congress have been weighing rules to crack down on that business. The government was also investigating Megaspeed for allegedly smuggling some Nvidia chips into China, in violation of U.S. law.

“There is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down,” Mr. Bessent said.

item.title: Jensen Huang Lost His Job. Wall Street Lost Its Biggest Prize.
item.description:
With Jensen Huang’s abrupt ouster from Nvidia, Wall Street has lost its most powerful and profitable dealmaker.

As Mr. Huang built Nvidia from a regional chipmaker into the world’s largest company, he dispensed with the usual careful, corporate hand-wringing. He personally directed splashy deals and complicated financing structures that pumped hundreds of billions of dollars into would-be competitors, suppliers and customers.

If that made him, in the public eye, a face of the global A.I. build out, on Wall Street he represented something else: manna. His deals produced billions of dollars in fees for banks’ asset managers and advisers, and Nvidia was, up until this week, spending or promising money at a speed and magnitude of little precedence.

Now Wall Street bankers, traders and even some of Nvidia’s competitors are wondering and worrying about whether Mr. Huang’s departure will slow the breakneck pace of Nvidia’s investments.

Some say that the fundamentals of Nvidia’s power are still intact, like its extreme control of the global supply of chips, the A.I. boom’s scarcest resource, the company’s deep cash coffers and the Trump administration’s warm support for the industry’s regulatory agenda. But Mr. Huang was the leader who harnessed all of those assets into a deal-making machine.

“Nvidia is the central bank of A.I.,” said Michael Edwards, director of Forum Markets, an A.I.-focused merchant bank. “Imagine the Fed without a chairman.”

Mr. Huang’s financial footprint is stamped all over the A.I. movement.

He steered tens of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s cash into bankrolling smaller A.I. companies — including Anthropic and OpenAI, helping them boom into the two behemoths of the space.

In August, Nvidia agreed to spend as much as $105 billion to back a giant data center in Ohio that is being built by SoftBank Energy and will be leased to OpenAI. At the time, Nvidia said it would offer financial guarantees for other data centers.

Through billions of investments, it has become part-owner of data-center companies such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren.

Nvidia has also struck deals to buy or effectively buy smaller competitors. Late last year, it said it would spend roughly $20 billion to license the technology of the chip start-up Groq and hire its top executive. In September, the company said it would buy Hugging Face, a library of open artificial intelligence models, for $12.9 billion.

Deals like that are the lifeblood of the financial world, producing fees for bankers and lawyers who charge thousands of dollars per hour. And Nvidia was increasingly reloading to do even more; this summer, with the help of three big banks, it completed its first bond offering in five years.

In turn, Wall Street firms were so enthusiastic to ingratiate themselves with Mr. Huang and Nvidia because he could mobilize other firms to spend hundreds of billions of dollars too, or at least promise to.

In one illustrative deal, Mr. Huang rang up David M. Solomon, Goldman Sachs’ chief executive, and others, with the idea that the bank and rivals assemble a joint consortium to lend to companies in need of expensive chips. Not a dime had been raised and even some inside the companies were unaware of it, when Mr. Huang nonetheless corralled the firms’ top brass in August to appear on CNBC and announce a half-trillion dollar target. Wall Street’s titans said they would do practically anything to help Mr. Huang keep the money rolling into A.I.

“This is calling all precincts” is how Apollo’s president, Jim Zelter, repeatedly described the effort during the CNBC appearance.

That financing initiative is in flux, according to three people involved in it but were not permitted to discuss the matter publicly. No loans have closed, and at least one of the six lenders that had agreed to it was on Thursday discussing dropping out, one of the people said.

That effort was signature Mr. Huang who, at seemingly every opportunity and with showmanlike style, carried the banner against technological doomerism and fatalism, arguing to continue to ratchet up the staggering pace of A.I. investment, a trend that became perhaps the singular underpinning for the stock market and broader economy.

With his trademark leather jacket, Mr. Huang consistently positioned himself and Nvidia as the industry’s model citizen and defender of A.I.’s importance to national security and America’s future.

He wasn’t shy to boast to financiers about his company’s importance. In March, after his company reported a $43 billion quarterly profit, Mr. Huang told an audience at Morgan Stanley that it was “the best quarter of earnings in the history of earnings,” and then a moment later expanded the time frame to “the history of humanity.” It was a lot of money, but not a record.

During his second administration, President Trump welcomed Mr. Huang and his policies into the White House. The two men have become close allies and used that alliance to bolster their respective agendas.

Still, not all hope has been lost on Wall Street. While Mr. Huang’s departure has prompted a sell off in Nvidia’s stock, stripping more than $1.5 trillion from its valuation, bankers and investors said that would not necessarily have negative implications for the initial public offering of the A.I. giant Anthropic still on track for next week.

Investors, optimistic market watchers said, did not sell all artificial intelligence stocks this week. Instead, they appear to be looking to diversify their A.I. investments away from Nvidia, potentially freeing up hundreds of billions of dollars to invest in Anthropic’s I.P.O.

The banks representing Anthropic on its I.P.O. are poised to generate more than $500 million in fees from its $1 trillion-plus listing.

item.title: Inside Microsoft’s Rush to Get Back Online After a Global Outage
item.description:
Late into the night Thursday, hundreds of Microsoft engineers and top executives were sitting in their darkened offices or home basements, logged into a video conference triaging a nightmare scenario for a technology company.

The world still runs on email, and much of that is processed through Microsoft Outlook. For hours, a company outage affected hospitals, schools, businesses and Congressional offices in Washington. Even Microsoft’s own staff couldn’t use email.

On the videoconference, Scott Guthrie, the senior most executive overseeing the company’s computing infrastructure, was proposing possible fixes, according to a person familiar with the call who was not authorized to speak publicly. People chewed on fingernails, rubbed their foreheads and debated how to turn off other services to prevent a “stampeding herd” so that as systems come back online, they would not be overwhelmed with new demands and shut back down.

By Friday morning, the company had apologized at least twice. It said it determined that the problem stemmed from a recent upgrade to its network, which shut down some servers, and that the systems were steadily improving. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” the company said in a statement. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

Finally, they had kept the herd at bay.

The prolonged and widespread outage was just the most recent reminder that the technological underpinnings of modern life and business are run through just a handful of major companies. And while cyberattacks and malicious actors can target their systems, sometimes the companies learn the hard way that they can introduce devastating flaws when updating or maintaining their own global systems.

Hospitals, law enforcement and government agencies and other vital services are often left vulnerable — unable to function for hours or days at a time.

Last year, Amazon’s cloud computing services were down for 15 hours and knocked a slew of apps and websites, including Zoom and parts of The New York Times, offline. And in the summer of 2024, a faulty software update by the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike caused airlines to ground flights, businesses to close early, and surgeries to be rescheduled.

For Microsoft, the problems from this week’s outage are not done yet. The short-term financial fallout should be “manageable,” analysts at the investment bank William Blair wrote in a research note Friday. But they said this prolonged outage is a reputational hit that could make companies and other customers reconsider having so much riding on one technology provider.

“We believe the outage could prompt enterprises to reassess their dependence on Microsoft’s infrastructure,” they wrote.

Outlook and other services affected, including Teams and its A.I. assistant Copilot, are part of Microsoft 365’s cloud subscription business, which is used by more than 450 million people and brought in almost $28 billion in its last quarter, which ended Sept. 30. Online memes joked the offering should be rebranded as Microsoft 364.

These subscriptions are central to the company’s business and the foundation on which it is promoting A.I. tools. Microsoft makes the case to customers that if they keep more data on Microsoft’s systems, they will be able to implement and maximize the benefits of A.I. more easily. Microsoft acknowledged that about 20 different services were impaired by the outage, a reminder that consolidating vendors can also create a bigger single point of failure.

Microsoft first detected the Outlook problems Thursday morning, around 9 a.m. on the West Coast, where the company is headquartered. It soon spread from the Americas around the world.

At first, the company said it thought the cause was an unexpected spike in traffic. Then it determined a large number of the company’s servers in its data centers were down, straining the rest of the system. Even as some servers were brought back online, they would shut down again, like a game of Whac-A-Mole.

Luca Arnaboldi, an assistant professor of cybersecurity at the University of Birmingham in England, said the outage was a reminder that when people use “the cloud,” they are actually relying on servers, which have finite resources.

On the overnight videoconference, Mr. Guthrie said while other systems were down too, the teams should prioritize restoring Outlook. Charles Lamanna, who heads many of Microsoft’s productivity services, was there too. He had already publicly apologized and said Microsoft had ruled out a cyberattack as the culprit.

The company’s own systems were to blame.

Isabella Kwai contributed reporting from London. Michael Levenson contributed reporting from New York.

item.title: How Wall Street Is Pitching Anthropic’s I.P.O.: ‘Too Crucial to Fail’
item.description:
On Friday afternoon, on the 56th floor of JPMorgan’s headquarters, Jamie Dimon interviewed perhaps the most important man to Wall Street right now: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic.

With less than one week before Anthropic plans to sell its shares on the open market, both men projected calm and confidence heading into what could be the largest initial public offering ever.

“We’re not super fussed on when exactly, what month, or what day, or what market conditions we go public into,” Dr. Amodei said, speaking on a small stage as thick clouds enveloped the New York skyline behind him.

Dr. Amodei’s nonchalance, though, belies the intensity of Wall Street’s efforts to sell Anthropic to investors. The company has lined up 22 banks, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, to run its “roadshow,” a series of meetings and presentations, where investors hear about the company’s financials.

Anthropic disclosed earlier this week it aimed to raise up to $100 billion at a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, down from $2 trillion bankers had floated this summer, before market jitters appeared.

JPMorgan and Citi are stewarding efforts to sell to individual investors, which Anthropic has said it expects to make up about 20 percent of the offering. Another critical group of investors: Seven of the tech industry’s biggest players, including Broadcom, Nvidia and Microsoft, which have already signed up to invest a total of $26 billion in Anthropic immediately after listing.

Each of those seven technology firms also stands to benefit from a successful Anthropic listing: Some, like Nvidia, Google and Microsoft, were already investors. All of them count Anthropic as a customer, and a successful Anthropic offering means a sustainable buyer of their services.

And the banks themselves could stand to collect roughly $400 million in fees on the deal, according to analysts at Evercore.

Anthropic is entering a market that has been less than ideal. Concerns about debt-fueled spending on artificial intelligence have whipsawed stock and bond prices for weeks. This week’s shocking resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive added more turmoil and uncertainty.

“Everyone has an interest in making this a success,” said Craig Coben, a former global head of equity capital markets at Bank of America, describing Anthropic’s offering as “too crucial to fail.”

“So far the market thinks the A.I. ecosystem can withstand Huang’s resignation,” Mr. Coben said, “but it’s still processing in real time what it all means for future spend and investment.”

Throughout its roadshow, Anthropic’s messaging has been that it will try to control its own destiny. In private meetings in New York conference rooms and on video calls, executives have stressed to investors that the company will rise above the fray by using a new cash pile from the I.P.O. to develop its own chips and build their own data centers.

They’re also selling what is, for now, a dream. Dr. Amodei has spent significant time in meetings on a subject without much traction yet: the company’s early forays into helping to develop new drugs and automate science laboratories, two investors said.

Anthropic, and its advisers, have taken a notably more austere approach than Elon Musk’s SpaceX public offering in June, a reflection in part of Dr. Amodei’s more understated style.

Mr. Musk’s roadshow video that opened with orchestral music, a snapshot of the moon, and reference to Mr. Musk’s goal to “change mankind and make us a multi-planetary species.”

In Anthropic’s promotional video, Dr. Amodei, sporting a teal sweater that went with the earthy colors of his office backdrop, warns within the first few minutes of the potential of artificial intelligence to “make a bioweapon or do a cyberattack.” (Dr. Amodei did call artificial intelligence “the most promising technology in human history” and closed the video by saying he thought A.I. would help end cancer and mental illness within a decade.)

For SpaceX’s I.P.O., which at the time was the largest on record, banks erected rocket ships in their lobbies and served space-themed food in their cafeterias to mark the first day of trading. During Friday’s roadshow event at JPMorgan, the bank handed out leather laptop cases and cookies that simply said “Anthropic.”

Some invisible Wall Street forces are working in Anthropic’s favor.

Because of its sizable valuation and new rules allowing large I.P.O.s to enter major stock indexes more quickly, the company will benefit from billions of dollars from passive index funds and exchange-traded funds that will automatically buy its shares in its early weeks of trading. That creates a can’t-miss feeling among investors who actively manage money and want to keep pace with the broader market.

Until now, Anthropic’s growth has also seeped into investors’ stock portfolios in more indirect ways. The A.I. company’s announcements have at times sent software stocks tumbling, for instance.

“It’s a must own because it’s a hedge against your existing portfolio,” said Jeremy Abelson, founder of Irving Investors, which buys private and public tech stocks.

Dr. Amodei isn’t a brand-new face for many large tech investors. The company raised more than $140 billion privately, including from some of the largest mutual funds, pension funds and sovereign wealth funds, much of it just this year.

Michael Paulus, founder of PCM Encore, a wealth management firm, compared the Anthropic I.P.O. to a promising early-stage start-up investment, on a much a grander scale.

“In the next 10 years, will Anthropic at some point trade down 70 percent, probably?” he said. “Could it be worth 10 times what it’s worth today? It’s also probably true.”

On Tuesday, Morgan Stanley hosted a meeting for investors with Anthropic’s chief financial officer, Krishna Rao. Next week, Mr. Rao and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic’s president and Mr. Amodei’s sister, will meet with investors at Goldman Sachs.

After his talk with Mr. Dimon on Friday, Mary Erdoes, who leads the bank’s asset and wealth management business, reiterated to the room what she deemed a key part of Dr. Amodei’s message.

“The goal is to under promise and to over deliver,” Ms. Erdoes said. “And we sure hope you do that.”

item.title: He Was China’s Man in Panama. Then He Became a Wanted Man.
item.description:
For years, Zhang Liang warned that powerful people in his former homeland, China, would try to drag him back. Then one Saturday morning in July, it happened.

In Panama City, two police officers on motorbikes pulled alongside his black Mercedes-Benz and motioned him to stop. A check of his identification turned up an Interpol red notice from the Chinese authorities, who wanted him extradited on charges of embezzling around $300 million.

Mr. Zhang, a 44-year-old dealmaker, barely had time to remove his gray suit jacket and wrap it around his head before officers handcuffed him and paraded him before cameras at Interpol’s National Central Bureau in Panama.

He has been behind bars ever since.

It was a remarkable fall for Mr. Zhang, one that traces the arc of China’s dealings with the West. He went to Panama ready to make deals and help China extend its influence. He oversaw a port project that promised to turn a former U.S. military base near the Panama Canal’s Atlantic entrance into Latin America’s largest container terminal, establishing a base for Chinese interests near one of the world’s busiest trade routes.

Today, China’s ruling Communist Party holds much tighter reins on entrepreneurs like Mr. Zhang. At the same time, Panama has been caught in a showdown between the United States and China: President Trump claims that China exercises too much control over the Panama Canal.

Mr. Zhang believes he is a pawn in a larger political game — a way for Beijing to regain direct control over key infrastructure he helped build in Panama.

“China is seeing its influence in the Panama Canal slipping away and is now putting pressure on Panama,” Mr. Zhang said from prison in a letter responding to written questions from The New York Times.

To his aggrieved former business partners, though, Mr. Zhang is a corporate fugitive who used offshore jurisdictions and other people’s money to enrich himself. He wooed Panama’s elite with promises of deals and funding that never materialized. He continued to earn a salary of $6,300 a month, his lawyers said at a bail hearing, a substantial sum in Panama.

His tailored suits, A. Lange & Söhne wristwatch and black Mercedes all pointed to a lavish lifestyle. Mr. Zhang has faced lawsuits, criminal complaints and judicial proceedings in multiple jurisdictions. He is also pursuing an international arbitration claim against Panama.

The competing accounts of victim and culprit are difficult to reconcile. The ownership of the port is disputed, and the financial dealings behind it are opaque. After reviewing the case, Panama’s Foreign Affairs Ministry agreed last month to proceed with Mr. Zhang’s extradition to China, according to a document seen by The Times.

The Foreign Affairs Ministries of China and Panama did not respond to emailed questions.

For a decade, Mr. Zhang had used China’s growing interest in Panama to expand his influence. Now, as Beijing and Washington battle over the canal, his business empire has unraveled, and the political connections that once helped him prosper offer little protection.

This account, with previously unreported details, is based on official documents, legal filings and interviews with lawyers and associates, including a former colleague who has accused local authorities in China of harassment, coercion and the falsifying of records in Mr. Zhang’s case.

Mr. Zhang arrived in Panama in 2016 to oversee investments for a wealthy Chinese financier. A lawyer licensed in New York and China, he had been named a “leading talent” by China’s Justice Ministry.

From an 18th-floor office overlooking Panama Bay, Mr. Zhang secured Panama’s approval to build, own and operate a major container terminal in a free-trade zone on Margarita Island.

Chinese state-controlled media celebrated the deal as a diplomatic coup, advancing investment interests in Panama. Mr. Zhang also secured a deal to build a gas-fired power plant. He promised officials that the project would create 1,000 jobs and lower energy costs.

As deals were made, Mr. Zhang became a go-between for officials in Beijing and Panama City.

His success coincided with Beijing’s courtship of Juan Carlos Varela, who was Panama’s president. In 2017, Panama severed diplomatic ties with Taiwan and aligned with China. It also became the first Latin American country to join the Belt and Road Initiative, China’s signature global infrastructure program.

Washington watched the growing relationship with alarm. Mr. Zhang’s proposed terminal would sit beside the Panama Canal, a strategic artery for the United States.

“Margarita Island gave them a lot of access and intelligence value,” said Isaac B. Kardon, an adjunct professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies who specializes in Chinese maritime strategy.

But the political opening started to close.

Mr. Varela left office in 2019, and his successor was far less receptive to Chinese investment. The Panamanian government began moving against the Margarita Island project.

Mr. Zhang sought Beijing’s help. Tingyun Han, his former assistant and translator, said she had gone to the Chinese Embassy in Panama City, hoping officials could persuade the Panamanian government to reconsider. The plea went nowhere.

The new Panamanian government “no longer wanted any Asian faces or Chinese enterprises involved,” Ms. Han told The Times from China.

Mr. Zhang’s problems deepened when his backer, a wealthy property financier named Gao Tianguo, lost his fortune. Mr. Gao’s lending businesses in China collapsed under billions of dollars of debt. He was arrested in 2020 and died two years later.

In 2022, Mr. Zhang agreed to transfer the port assets to Notarc Management Group, a Bahamas and Florida-based private equity firm. Within months, the deal incited an ownership dispute. Ye Cheng, a politically connected Chinese businessman who claimed a controlling stake in the project, accused Mr. Zhang of illegally seizing the company.

But Panamanian authorities declined to bring charges, concluding that Mr. Ye’s allegations amounted to a commercial dispute. Mr. Ye’s company, the Landbridge Group, did not reply to requests for comment.

China took a different view.

In 2023, police officers pulled Ms. Han, Mr. Zhang’s former assistant, off a plane in her home city of Xian and drove her 12 hours to Rizhao, where Mr. Ye’s company has its headquarters, she said. Officers interrogated her so intensely about Mr. Zhang and the port deal, she said, that she vomited and was taken to a hospital. She later accused the local police of torture.

Mr. Zhang became convinced that his adversaries in China were coming after him. In court filings in 2024, he described being followed to work by a white Nissan and chased through Panama City. He requested and received police protection.

By the time the police stopped Mr. Zhang’s Mercedes in July, Panama had become the focus of tensions between Washington and Beijing.

Shortly after starting his second term, President Trump demanded that Panama loosen China’s grip on the Panama Canal. He accused a Hong Kong conglomerate that operated two major ports at the canal, one at either end, of being controlled by Beijing. In January, Panama’s Supreme Court declared the company’s port contract unconstitutional.

China vowed to “take all necessary measures” to defend its interests in Panama. Chinese authorities started detaining hundreds of Panamanian-flagged vessels in China for inspection, disrupting trade.

Mr. Zhang was arrested the same week that China’s new ambassador arrived in Panama — and just five days before Panamanian officials were due in Beijing for talks to defuse the diplomatic standoff.

Panama’s foreign minister later said China had renewed a key maritime agreement that grants Panamanian-flagged ships preferential access to its ports.

“From the moment they arrested him — and that is no coincidence — the disputes between China and Panama disappeared,” said Guillermo Cochez, a Panamanian diplomat and one of Mr. Zhang’s lawyers.

No evidence links his arrest to the diplomatic negotiations. But relations between China and Panama improved afterward. Extradition documents revealed that Beijing wanted control of Mr. Zhang’s assets in Panama without explicitly asking for the port project.

On Aug. 21, a Panamanian court denied Mr. Zhang bail and ruled that the seriousness of the charges outweighed his claims of personal roots in Panama. In September, Panama’s Foreign Ministry said China’s extradition request was “appropriate.”

Mr. Zhang was moved from La Gran Joya, a high-security prison outside Panama City, to another detention center nearby, while his lawyers pursue a final appeal.

China has said Mr. Zhang is a Chinese national, although he said he had renounced his Chinese citizenship and obtained citizenship from Saint Lucia in 2020. The Times reviewed copies of his permanent residency card, his Saint Lucia passport and his Chinese passport.

Chinese authorities said Mr. Zhang’s transfer of the port terminal to Notarc had constituted embezzlement. He dismissed the allegations as a “sham.” (Notarc also sued him, seeking compensation for losses it says it incurred in the dispute.) Notarc did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Zhang said the criminal case was a pretext for Beijing to seize the Margarita Island project and “get back into the canal.”

But, he warned, “what Panama doesn’t realize is the pressure won’t stop with extraditing me.”
